name: Fatima Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Fatima, thanks for talking to me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both the public version and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for an outsourcing company that runs customer service for a mobile phone network. So the customers think they're talking to the network, but my payslip says a different company. Mostly I do live chat, three chats at once, sometimes calls when the phones get busy. It's roaming charges, broken phones, people who want to leave and need to be talked into staying.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the chats where someone's furious and by the end they say thank you with a smiley. What wears me out is the retention target, because I'm meant to keep a certain number of people from cancelling and I'm bad at it. I've been there just over a year and I'm still below the line most months. My partner Tomás works nights as a nurse, so I come home to a quiet flat and cook for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, so basically the world we have now. I can picture that easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now the companies will stop pretending a chatbot is customer service. To friends I'd joke that my job's safe until the next outsourcing contract. Online I might share something about workers being right not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thing that scares me at work isn't AI, it's the contract. The network could move us to another outsourcer or overseas whenever the deal ends next spring. And the small AI bits, like the suggested replies in the chat window, will still be used to push us to take four chats at once instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try to get above the retention line, because that's what keeps you safe when contracts change. I'd keep my savings where they are, about three months. I've used the suggested replies now and then, so I'd use them a bit more if it helped my numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I guess. Not because of AI. Because I never know if the contract renews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the contract comes up next spring, what actually happens on the floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone gets twitchy. Last time the rumours started in January, the managers stopped saying anything, and people started looking at other jobs on their lunch breaks. Two of my friends from training left before we even knew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it did go, what's your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are other contact centres in town, a bank and an insurer, so I'd apply there. Tomás earns steady money at the hospital, so we wouldn't go under. But I'd hate starting from the bottom again after a year of learning this system.

say: I'd say companies should **stop pretending** a chatbot is real customer service.
I'd joke my job is safe until the **next outsourcing contract**.
think: The real risk is the network **moving the contract** when it ends next spring.
Small AI tools will still be used to push **four chats** at once.
do: Work to get above the **retention target** before the contract review.
Use the **suggested replies** a little more to help her numbers.
Leave her **three months** of savings untouched.
feel: **Uneasy** about the contract, not about the technology.
S0.quote: The thing that scares me at work isn't AI, it's the contract. The network could move us to another outsourcer or overseas whenever the deal ends next spring.
fieldNote: Her insecurity comes from **outsourcing**, which exists with or without AI.
Her partner's **hospital wage** gives the household a floor she relies on.
She talks about AI tools as **target pressure** more than as a threat to her job.

steps.text: Get above the retention target before next spring's contract review
Use the chat window's suggested replies more on busy shifts
Keep three months of savings untouched in case the contract ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's closer to home. Answering customers is literally my job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at work and online: if a company replaces half its customer service with bots, it should have to retrain the people it lets go. I'd probably post about it, which I don't usually do. I'd also tell my team to get the union talking to the outsourcer, because we only have a few members.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think chat is the first thing to go. A bot can do three chats, or three hundred. Phone calls with angry people might last longer, but I'm on chat most of the time, and my numbers aren't good enough to be kept when they shrink the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd move myself onto the phones as much as I could, because people who call are often the hard cases. I'd join the union, and I'd look at the healthcare admin course Tomás keeps mentioning, the one for booking patients at the hospital. I'd also learn the AI tools properly, but only after seeing which ones the good agents actually use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling-apart anxious, more like a low hum all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said healthcare admin. Isn't booking also on that list of thinking tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I thought of that while I was saying it. Booking is booking. But hospitals move slowly, and patients are scared people who need a voice on the phone, so I think healthcare admin would take longer. It's not a forever plan, it's a five-year plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership, which I barely use anyway. And we were planning a trip to see my grandparents next summer, which we'd still do, but cheaper. I'd keep the savings for whatever comes next.

say: I'd say firms that replace staff with bots must **pay for retraining**.
I'd push my team to get the **union** talking to the outsourcer.
think: **Chat goes first**, because a bot can handle hundreds at once.
My **numbers** aren't good enough to survive a smaller team.
do: Ask to move onto **phone shifts**, where the hard cases still need people.
Join the **union** and look at a **healthcare admin** course.
Learn the **AI tools** the best agents already use.
feel: **Anxious**, like a low hum that never quite stops.
S1.quote: Hospitals move slowly, and patients are scared people who need a voice on the phone, so I think healthcare admin would take longer.
fieldNote: She **catches her own contradiction** about booking and owns it calmly.
Her steady style shows: she'd **copy proven tools**, not experiment first.
She expects to lose **chat work** but feels some control through planning.

steps.text: Request phone shifts instead of chat to handle harder cases
Join the union and push it to talk to the outsourcer
Look into the hospital's patient booking admin course
Cancel the gym and plan a cheaper trip to her grandparents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's shocking. That's before my next contract cycle is even over twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this has to be managed by governments, not by companies racing each other. I'd sign up for any campaign for a basic income or a jobs guarantee. At work, I'd say what everyone would be thinking: we're done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job ends in 2027 or 2028, and the healthcare admin idea dies with it, because that's thinking work too. The only thing that buys time is hands-on work, and that's what Tomás does. Nursing has robots coming three years later, and even then people will want a human to hold their hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a healthcare assistant course right away, the hands-on kind, washing and feeding patients, because it uses the three-year gap. I'd save every spare bit, maybe stop eating out entirely. We'd also stop talking about a bigger flat and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And kind of hollow, because I just spent a year learning a system that won't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Tomás that I'm going to follow him into the hospital, so please don't laugh. He'd be pleased, I think, but he'd also tell me the shifts are brutal and the pay's not much more. We'd sit at the kitchen table with a calculator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger brother, who's nineteen and just started a call centre job because I told him it was decent. I'd feel responsible. I'd tell him to get out before me.

say: I'd say governments must manage this, not **companies racing** each other.
I'd back any campaign for a **basic income** or jobs guarantee.
think: My job ends by **2028**, and admin work goes with it.
Hands-on care buys **three more years**, and people still want a human there.
do: Start a **healthcare assistant** course straight away.
Stop eating out and **save every spare bit** of pay.
Put the plan for a **bigger flat** on hold.
feel: **Alarmed** at losing her job within two years.
**Hollow** about a year spent learning a system that will vanish.
S2.quote: I'd tell my partner Tomás that I'm going to follow him into the hospital, so please don't laugh.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **admin is thinking work** and drops that plan.
Her partner's **nursing career** becomes her map for what to do next.
Guilt over her **younger brother** shows how she thinks about others.

steps.text: Enrol in a healthcare assistant course this year
Stop eating out and save every spare bit of pay
Shelve the plan to rent a bigger flat with Tomás
Sign up to a campaign for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but it's different. You could actually do something with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to get the rules right, so let's not waste them. I'd tell people at work to start learning something now. I'd probably still post things about workers needing a voice in this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd have two or three good years left on the phones, then it thins out. Five years is enough to get a healthcare qualification without panic, and the robots wouldn't come for care work until about 2034. So I'd lose this job but probably not my living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd stay at work and do the healthcare assistant course part time, evenings and weekends. I'd try the AI tools more at work to keep my numbers up while I'm still there. And I'd keep saving, maybe get to five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but I can see the steps. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lose the job but not your living. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, I just think caring for sick people will be one of the last things we hand over. Even if a robot can lift a patient, someone needs to notice they're frightened. Tomás says half his job is that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who said you were giving up on customer service too early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody at my company gets promoted out of chat anyway. So I'd say I'm not giving up on customer service, I'm getting out before the door shuts. I'd rather leave on my own terms than in a meeting room with a box.

say: I'd say we have a few years to **get the rules right**.
I'd tell coworkers to **start learning** something new now.
think: I'd get two or three years on the phones before it **thins out**.
Care work buys time until about **2034**, so I'd keep a living.
do: Study a **healthcare assistant** course part time while still working.
Use **AI tools** at work to protect her numbers meanwhile.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier because she can see the **steps**.
S3.quote: I'm not giving up on customer service, I'm getting out before the door shuts. I'd rather leave on my own terms than in a meeting room with a box.
fieldNote: Five years turns her plan from **panic** into a **schedule**.
She trusts that **human care** lasts longer than robots can match.
Leaving on her **own terms** matters to her as much as money.

steps.text: Take a part-time healthcare assistant course on evenings and weekends
Use the chat assistant tools to keep her numbers up
Build savings up to about five months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Honestly, that's long enough to have a whole other career started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for governments and unions to set things up properly, training funds, notice periods, all of it. I'd say it calmly, because ten years doesn't feel like an emergency. I'd still tell my brother to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably stay in customer service a few more years and see what really happens, because things change. I'd want to see if the tools actually get that good. But I'd want a second option ready before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short first aid and care course in year one to test whether I even like that kind of work. I'd volunteer at a care home a few Saturdays to find out. I'd keep my job, keep the union card, and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More relaxed. I'd still think about it, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see if the tools get that good. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the network let a bot handle the cancellations, the hardest chats, and the complaints didn't go up, that's when I'd know. Until then I'd keep testing other things on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any bit of this future you'd look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the bot takes the roaming-charge chats, that's fine by me, they're boring. I just want there to be something human left for people like me to do.

say: I'd say governments and unions must set up **training funds** and notice periods.
I'd tell my brother **to plan**, calmly, without panic.
think: I'd stay a few years and **see what happens** first.
I'd want a **second option** ready well before 2036.
do: Take a short **first aid and care** course in the first year.
Volunteer some Saturdays at a **care home** to test the work.
Keep her job, her **union card** and her savings plan.
feel: **Relaxed** enough to sleep, though it stays on her mind.
S4.quote: If the network let a bot handle the cancellations, the hardest chats, and the complaints didn't go up, that's when I'd know.
fieldNote: Her steady side comes out: she wants **proof** before committing.
She would **test care work** cheaply before betting on it.
She still expects her **chat job** to end, just not soon.

steps.text: Take a short first aid and care course in year one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it leaves no time to switch, and my brother is in the same job. What would help is a paid retraining scheme where you get part of your wage while you train for care or another hands-on job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about outsourcing. Even without AI, people like me live contract to contract. The chatbot just makes it easier for the network to drop us without anyone noticing.

headlineQuote: The chatbot just makes it easier for the network to drop us without anyone noticing.
portrait: Fatima is 27 and does **live chat** for a mobile network through an outsourcing firm.
She's below her **retention target** and lives contract to contract.
Her partner is a **night-shift nurse**, and she keeps eyeing care work as her way out.
She waits for **proof** before trying new tools but plans carefully once convinced.
She blames **outsourcing and firms** more than AI and wants paid retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to switch and her **brother** works in call centres too.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining scheme** that covers part of her wage while she trains for care work.
